utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today's the 20th of May, 2008. Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon, Defence counsel. My greetings to the accused and to all the people helping us out. And my greetings to the Prosecution as well. I'm going to read out three oral rulings, they are numbered. Ruling number one, in relation to the status of the statement by Accused Prlic. On 6th of May, 2008, the Prosecution asked the Trial Chamber to lift the confidentiality of Exhibit P 09078, the statement made by the accused Prlic. It was admitted by the Trial Chamber on the 22nd of August, 2007. There was no objection from the Defence teams. In as much as the Trial Chamber has never ordered the said exhibit to be under seal, the request is moot. The Trial Chamber will ask the registrar to make sure that in the e-court database Exhibit P 09078 is, indeed, a public exhibit. Ruling number two, oral ruling in relation to the application by the Prosecution regarding 65 ter (G) summaries. On the 6th and on the 19th of May, 2008, the Prosecution firstly asked for the Prlic Defence to provide written statements of Defence witnesses. Secondly, that the summaries provided further to Rule 65 ter (G) be completed. The Prlic Defence objected. Firstly, the Trial Chamber recalls that unlike the Prosecution, the Defence is under no obligation to obtain written statements from witnesses it plans to call for their Defence case. Further to Rule 67 (A), the only obligation for the Defence is to disclose statements it has in its possession. Therefore, the Trial Chamber denies the first application. With regard to summaries under Rule 65 ter (G), the Trial Chamber points out that the Prosecution had an opportunity to make submissions during the pre-Defence Conference on the 21st of April, 2008. It recalls that the Prosecution offered an agenda for specific items to be discussed that were connected with the filing of Rule 65 ter (G) lists without, however, raising the issue of which the Trial Chamber has now been seized. The Trial Chamber also points out that the quality of the summaries differs from one witness to the other. Therefore, there is no need to ask for further information on a systematic basis with regard to all or any statements provided under Rule 65 ter (G). The Trial Chamber therefore denies the second application. This being said, the Trial Chamber will on a case-by-case basis require further information and additional information in relation to summaries if it so deems necessary, which is going to be the case in ruling number three. Oral ruling related to Witness Zdravko Sancevic and requests for further information to be obtained from the Prlic Defence. In view of the testimony on the 26th to the 29th of April -- of May, 2008, the Trial Chamber examined the summary of the testimony by Zdravko Sancevic, a Prlic Defence witness. The Trial Chamber is of the view that some of the information provided in the summary is vague and lack precision. For instance, the summary says that the witness moved from Medjugorje to Sarajevo or went from Medjugorje to Sarajevo in 1993 in order to speak with the BiH authorities. The summary fails to specify the purpose of the meeting or meetings, how often they took place or when they took place exactly. On the other hand, the witness was -- apparently attended a meeting in Medjugorje on the 18th of May or July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in which Mr. Prlic allegedly -- I shall repeat. On the 18th of May, meeting at which Mr. Prlic was regarded as: "The perfect candidate for the three parties." Following the meeting, the witness is purported to have had contacts with Mr. Prlic as the representative of BiH. The Prlic Defence has, however, failed to state when the meeting took place exactly. It only said that it took place on the 18th of May. The Prlic Defence did not either mention the positions Mr. Prlic would have been appointed to. The Trial Chamber is of the view that additional information would make it possible for the Trial Chamber to be better prepared for the future testimony of the witness and would make it possible for the Prosecution and the other Defence teams to prepare for their cross-examination. Therefore, further to or in keeping with the oral ruling issued today, the Trial Chamber invites the Prlic Defence to provide the necessary additional information to complement the statement -- the summary of the testimony of Zdravko Sancevic. No further ruling. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed. You have two hours and one minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that we don't have e-court for my colleague here and she's probably the most valuable member of the Defence team, much more than I am. So if we could have some assistance from the technical booth. While that's being done, Your Honour, by Thursday we hope to provide the additional information requested with respect to the following witness. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too, Mr. Karnavas, and to everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have only two hours. I had asked for an additional hour, but hopefully in two hours we will be able to do our work. So I would ask you to please, please keep your answers rather short, direct, and then if I need more clarification I'll ask for that. If we could go now to the next document, 1D 02624, 2624. As everyone recalls from yesterday we left off when we were speaking about reports, the fact that you had prepared reports and indeed that you did prepare reports which were shared with the international community and others. So if we look at 2624, for the record we see that this is a report dated 14th of October 1994. On the first page we see your name, and then later on if we look through the report again we see at the end of the text, before we get to the charts, we see your name again. My first question is: Are you aware of this document? Have you seen it before? I'll wait for you to get it. 26 --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this document and I've seen it before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we see in this document lots of data. Can you tell us how this data was collected and how this report was compiled?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was compiled by the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons -- actually, this is the final analysis based on the census of all the refugees and displaced persons containing all the most important elements that concern the care for all of our refugees and displaced persons. The report was sent to the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, with which we had a very close cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would this report have also been shared with UNHCR, the EU, and others, to your knowledge and understanding?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was sent to the President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman; to the Prime Minister, Mr. Nikica Valentic; and the Deputy Prime Minister, Dr. Nikola Kostovic. I only assume but I'm not absolutely sure that it was also copied to UNHCR. As soon as UNHCR found out that there was a report of that sort they would ask for it, so I assume that they would be copied. When it comes to the official sending of the report, it was done to the first three addressees that I mentioned because they were the ones most concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then yesterday we touched upon this, but who paid for this report to be done? Was this money from the government or did you get also money from outside agencies, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was done by the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons in which there were persons who compiled it who were on the payroll by the Government of the Republic of Croatia. Let's just say that the lists of all refugees and displaced persons on that year as well as the year before were funded by the UNHCR and the Government of the Republic of Croatia jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now if we go to the next document, 1D 02628, 2628, that's the very next document in your binder, do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it, Mr. Karnavas. This is a document that was published in our gazette, that we occasionally published. It was done other annually or twice every year, and this gazette was dispatched to all humanitarian organizations, to the media, and to all the government offices. It was a public document featuring data to inform our general public as to what we were doing, how we were doing it, how many refugees and displaced persons we had, and how much it all cost and how the costs were borne by the Government of the Republic of Croatia on the one hand and how it was financed from the funds provided to us from the UNHCR and the European Union. This document also provides detailed data as to how many males, how many females, how many children were among the refugees and displaced persons, how many were children, how many were sick, how many were able-bodied, how many were not. A lot of data that the general public might find useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just a couple of points, and again very quickly because the Judges may have some questions on this report. But if we look at -- it's the page after page number 4, Your Honours. It doesn't have a page number but it would be found after page number 4. At the top we see it says: "Status and rights of displaced persons and refugees." Do you see that, sir? Have you found that page?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I have the page in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what this page is referring to, if I'm correct, if we look at this is the law that was being applied by your office at the time with respect to granting status to both displaced persons and refugees coming from BiH, and this place obviously generated from the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, Mr. Karnavas. This is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could turn to another page, it's toward the latter part of the or the middle of the report and I'll just read these -- I guess it's an ERN number, it's 1D 34 and it's 0596, so the last four numbers, Your Honours, 0596, where we see at the top -- we'll have to turn the document over. Usher, if we could have the assistance of the usher and we'll be requesting your assistance throughout the afternoon. So if you could -- but we have it here for the -- because of the time constraints, I appreciate your assistance. If we see at the top it says -- if we turn it over -- turn it around: "Number of registered displaced persons and refugees since the beginning of 1995." And on this very same page we see 1993 and we have broken it down into months. So we're able to see displaced persons, refugees, and the total number. My first question regarding this, Dr. Rebic, is: Where do these numbers come from?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These numbers, Mr. Karnavas, come from the different censuses of refugees and displaced persons done on various years. We had a census in 1992, 1993, and 1994. Our regional offices and centres for social welfare regularly sent data every month to the central office at the government so that we knew exactly how the numbers of refugees and displaced persons changed from one month to another. We published that. First we informed the government and the ministry that we cooperated with on these issues, but then we also provided the data to the media and to the general public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And I point this out for Your Honours so you can trace whether the borders were closed and to see the in-flow of refugees and what have you. Unless there are any questions I'm going to move on to other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a follow-up question, Witness. Please look at this chart just pointed out to us by Mr. Karnavas, the ERN number ends with 0596. We see the chart for 1992, 1993, and then 1994 and 1995. It's a very interesting chart because it sums up the situation with regard to displaced persons and refugees. Indeed, we have a column devoted to displaced persons and another to refugees. Look at the refugee column, that's what I'm interested in, because if you go by the definition of a refugee it is a person who's not of Croatian nationality and enters the territory of Croatia. I have questions because of the figures between the numbers and the flows. There is a rise, as we can see, as to the flow because in 1992 in January we have 872 refugees and then around 1200 in February, in March it goes up to 16.000, and then there's a peak in April, 193.000. And then we have a number that keeps increasing until it sort of stagnates around 350.000 and above. And then curiously enough, in 1993 we have a base of 400.000 in January, and that amount is going to drop as months go by. Look at December, indeed, then there are only 281.318 refugees. So I guess we have to read these numbers in terms of stocks and flows. For somebody who knows about statistics, who knows about stocks and flows, one has the impression that the situation as of July 1992 stabilizing in terms of stocks and that there's not going to be any new refugees. On the contrary, we're going to see a drop in the number of refugees. Do you have any comments of your own, because after all you are the specialist in this matter since you were the head of the office. So I suppose -- I guess this didn't escape you. So what can you say as to the interpretation that can be given of these figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 1992, in the month of April, was the beginning of a very fierce aggression of the former JNA commanded by the Serb officers, and this is the time when the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in the occupied territory started fleeing in large numbers. And that's why in the month of April all of a sudden we had such a high figure, all of a sudden 193.000. The aggression was stepped up and the army managed to occupy large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina very quickly. That's why every month we had an increasing number of refugees coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The largest number of refugees was recorded towards the end of that year, in November and December, and then in 1993 in January, February, and March. With the beginning of spring 1993, some of the refugees managed to return to their homes and some were taken on by third countries, for example, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway. That is why in 1993 the number settled around 270.000, but then again in May, June, and July the number went up again because we again saw refugees coming from Central Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the number was on the rise again all the way up to the end of 1993. And then in 1994, after the month of April, again in spring, the number started falling. And as the situation in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became calmer and featured a smaller number of threats, the Bosnian refugees started going back home so that towards the end of 1994 the number of refugees stabilized around 180 or 190.000 and that number remained constant up to the Operation Storm as of September and October 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you here. I've had a look at tables 1994 and 1995, and apparently there is a stock of, a minimum of 100.000 to 200.000 refugees because in June 1995 we have 188.606, that's roughly 200.000 people. If we deduct that from the period at the heart of the indictment, from January to December 1993, with a stock of roughly 300.000, if we assume that there is a stock, basic stock, of 200.000 and refugees of -- amounting to 270.000 to 300.000 people, does it mean that in 1993 we have 100.000 refugees who came to Croatia? Would that be a mistake, considering all the other figures that actually 100.000 refugees arrived in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of 1993 the number of refugees decreased, contrary to what you're saying, so that the 400.000 refugees in January started dwindling. In the month of May and June, the numbers increased again from 269.000 in the month of April to 271.000 in May, and then in June to 272.000, and then in July to 277. So again in the course of these months the number didn't go down but it gradually went up. This also refers to the refugees who arrived in the Republic of Croatia again, and that's where we had to accommodate them, in the Republic of Croatia. And finally, the number stabilized somewhat around the 180.000 mark in 1994, in the month of August, that was displaced persons; and 296.000 was the number of refugees, and those numbers remained constant up to Operation Storm in August 1995. After Operation Storm a huge number of both refugees and displaced persons managed to return home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll stop here because we could spend hours on these tables. I just wanted you to confirm for us that in 1993 the number of refugees gradually decreased. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, picking up from that, during that period were refugees and displaced persons also leaving from the Republic of Croatia to third countries? In other words, we have these figures, but do these figures also reflect whether during that period you have refugees leaving so that some leave, others are coming in, taking up those spots, hence we have these particular figures? Can you help us out on that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, Mr. Karnavas. There was a constant movement of both refugees and displaced persons from the Republic of Croatia to third countries. UNHCR in 1993 largely took it upon themselves to deal with people from Bosnia and Herzegovina with our help and they took them to third countries with our transit visa. Those were people whom UNHCR helped directly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, took them over, and sent them to third countries. In 1993 UNHCR also helped people in the Republic of Croatia and took some refugees and displaced persons to third countries with a desire to facilitate the burden upon the Republic of Croatia. At that time we were simply exhausted, our resources were lacking and we were exhausted with the care.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to go through very quickly a series of other documents. We've seen them last week with Mr. Zoric, but I just want some confirmation from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And these documents, I'm going to read them and then we're going to go just very briefly with one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 1D 02585, if you could just look at that to start with. Do you recognise this document? We see your name at the bottom, although by now all of us will be able to recognise that this is not your signature.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, that is correct. I recognise the document. The document was signed by the secretary of the Office of Refugees and Displaced Persons, Mr. Josip Esterajher, who himself was a displaced person from Vukovar, a journalist by trade. In the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons he was dealing with informing and acted as a liaison officer with the media. From time to time he also reported the -- to the media about the situation concerning refugees and displaced persons, especially their numbers, how many they are, where they are accommodated, in which county, in which towns, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go to the next document, 1D 02590. And the first thing I would like you to do is go to the third page, page number 3. You will see at the end of the text, the typed text, there seems to be something handwritten. Do you recognise that, what's handwritten on page 3? It looked like initials.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise, this is a facsimile of my name and family name which I usually used when I signed the students' books. Instead of always signing by hand I had a facsimile of my signature that I used to sign my students' books with. I'm familiar with the document. This must have been part of my report or a presentation, and it deals with the issues of welfare and looking after refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we don't have a date for this document, but if I could focus your attention on the first paragraph on page 1, we see that it relates to August 14th to September 23, we admitted 21.000 refugees from BH and FRY, F-R-Y. Now, based on that --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because FRY stands for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, can you give us an approximation what year might this document was generated?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was probably compiled towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go to the next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but just counsel could -- the document itself on the first page refers to 1994. So I'm not sure how it could be written in 1992. In 1994 390.000, 9 per cent information, that's -- I'm not sure how the document could have been created in 1992 if that assists the witness or he can assist us further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the paper -- that's in the third paragraph, but with relation to the first paragraph I guess these figures are related too -- this would be 1992, the first paragraph, that is, these figures because we're talking about FRY.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the year is mentioned here [In English] 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you are right, sir, there's also reference made to 1993 and 1994. So this is a summary which I suppose must have been compiled in 1994, you're right. Since there is no date, this was not an official document which may be seen from my signature and which I only used to confirm that this was my document and the document was probably used during my -- one of my lectures. I often appeared on TV, on radio, I appeared at various conferences and congresses abroad, and I would take one of these reports with me that I had compiled and that I then kept in my private files. So from the integrity of the report one can conclude that this was the end of 1994, but the document concerns the entire duration of the refugee crisis starting with the beginning of 1992 to the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, something came to my mind listening to you. We have a large number of refugees were accommodated in various centres. Did the media have access easily to these refugees? Were they interviewed? Were they able to tell their stories? Or did the office or the Government of the Republic of Croatia restrict access by the media to refugees, or did the media have access to the refugees without any problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The media were supposed to have a permit from our office to go and visit refugee camps and do interviews there. It would, however, happen every now and then that they went there without such a permit. We did not create any problems as a result of that, and that's how some media would do similar interviews that would then create certain tensions in the press, be it Croatian or foreign press, because sometimes they would interview those refugees or those displaced persons who were particularly vulnerable, particularly stressed out, and such persons - I've had experiences of that sort myself - such persons would provide not only subjective statements about the situation but also they would paint a whole picture in very negative colours. I can give you a number of examples of the experiences that I had with my own co-citizens, refugees, they would complain about soup not being good, bread being hard, meat being of not good quality. This is all very much understandable when you know that you are dealing with people who are stressed out and who had had negative experiences before they first arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I was not talking about any restrictions with respect to their life in Croatia. My question related to what could have happened to them in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example. That's what I was interested in. Did you exercise any control on interviews given by these people when talking about what happened to them before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was, but let me start by first things first. When the refugees and displaced persons were registered in 1994 [as interpreted], each person was interviewed, asking them to provide their personal data, and also statements were taken from them as to what they had been through in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what they had lost, who had been killed, and similar things. And there is also a survey carried out by the PULS agency, a survey done in the media and among the refugees about the situation among the refugees and especially among the citizens of Croatia and their attitude towards refugees and displaced persons. This was also done without permit because that agency had asked for our permission to carry out such a survey. However, people would enter refugee and displaced persons centres even without our permission because we just could not exercise a firm control. So representatives of different media, German television, Arabic television, entered those centres. They were supposed to report to the head of such a centre first, they did, and then they interviewed people, but it was impossible to control who was being interviewed and what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One correction and then some follow-up on that. I believe on line -- page 16, line 20 it should be 1991 as opposed to 1994, where they began taking the census. Following up on the questions asked of you, having lived through the former Yugoslavia during the Tito era when the press was censored to some extent or controlled by the state, did you in any way try to censor what the media, the free media, at the time was writing? Did you try to control what they were publishing as a result of interviews that they might have had with displaced persons or refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, it was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the permission ever granted to enter these centres on the condition that they had to publish positive news or at least allow you or your staff or your office or some government official to look at the material, what was going to be published, before it could actually go to press and to the public?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We trusted the media, including those coming from abroad as well as those who were in the Republic of Croatia. They enjoyed our trust and we let them choose whether they would paint a favourable picture or a negative one. We never put any conditions before them or asked them to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You indicated yesterday that you often went abroad and on some occasions you had visited sites where refugees were being held, such as in Hungary, for instance, Germany. When you would visit those sites, could you just go there unannounced or did you need permission from the particular government that was running the centre?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Each time I went there on behalf of the Office for Displaced Persons and on behalf of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, be it in situations when I visited Slovenia, Germany, or other countries, I had to come announced which is only understandable. And in such cases I usually received an escort, without which I wouldn't have been able to enter any refugee centres. I always had an escort with me and they would explain to me how they went about taking care of the people, and I find it only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday also, just one last follow-up question on this whole topic, yesterday you indicated that there were times when you visited centres in the Republic of Croatia with foreign dignitaries. I believe you indicated on one occasion it was the head of UNHCR. On those occasions, did you restrict movement of those dignitaries? Did you prevent them at any point on visiting whatever sites they wanted to visit and whatever sites inside the particular centres? In other words, was it choreographed so that in advance you could paint a rosy picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm going to continue to object, I haven't this afternoon yet, but continuous leading questions and suggestive questions, Your Honour. There's a very easy to ask this question in a proper way and that is: What was the policy of your office in connection with press access to so and so? What was the policy of your office in connection with visits by certain officials? But these questions over and over and over again are directive, suggesting, they're argumentive, and I wish the Chamber would intervene so that I wouldn't have to intervene all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond. Normally in many situations in other Chambers, questions from the Bench come at the very end. Here we welcome these sorts of questions at times because they're relevant to the topic. When a series of questions is requested from the Bench they're required further follow-up, in essence the line of questioning amounts to re-direct; hence, there is in the process of re-direct a certain amount of leading. However, if it bothers the Prosecution I will try to refrain from that approach. But I don't see any purpose how that is served -- the purpose that is -- because yesterday the gentleman indicated on direct that Mrs. Ogata went to a particular location with him. Now the follow-up was: Was she restricted once she got there? How is that in any way leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not re-direct, it's not re-direct. This is direct examination in any event. For an example, and it's about to leave the screen, Mr. Karnavas after a long directive speech then concludes with: "In other words, was it choreographed so that in advance you could paint a rosy picture?" Now, that is clearly argumentive, there's no reason for it. If I have to object every time, then that's what I'll do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, to avoid objections, you should have asked -- with respect to the visits by foreign officials, you should have asked whether foreign officials had visited these centres with the witness, he would have said, and then you moved on to something else. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next series of documents -- I'm told that we are -- we should get an answer from the witness. Can you please tell us, I know you said yesterday, but can you re-tell us, did foreign dignitaries visit centres in the Republic of Croatia? And to phrase the question with the words stipulated by the Prosecution: What was the procedure once they got the there?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Scott, we had frequent visits by diplomats, politicians, senior humanitarian officials. They would come and visit our refugee centres. Among those high officials, for example, was President Demirel, Mrs. Ogata, and other prime ministers and ministers. I was always with them, and in case I was absent they would be escorted by Mr. Granic. They were free to move about the refugee centre. The only point when they needed me was at the gate. I had to introduce them into the camp, otherwise they would have had to jump the fence. Frequently I would tell them, Now we're inside, feel free to walk around and ask questions of anyone you meet. I remember that Ms. Sadako Ogata at a refugee centre near Kutina, and I think it was Sweden or Denmark that had built the centre, I remember her visiting that centre. I showed her the buildings there. And finally she told me, Now I would like to address some people, to talk to them, but I want to choose the bungalow and I want to speak to whoever I want to. And she picked one bungalow and went inside. In that particular bungalow we had displaced persons alongside some refugees. She accidentally came upon a Vukovar family. There was an elderly lady there with a son of hers who was about 40 years old and had suffered severe stress. Ms. Ogata asked that old lady whether she hated the Serbs for what they had done to her, and she said, Ma'am, definitely not. I pray that my son will never find it necessary to revenge his father's and his brothers' death so that I can face God with a clean conscience. I also remember Mr. Zimmerman, who was the US ambassador to the former Yugoslavia, I took him to a displaced persons centre. He also asked questions of people he met along the way. I didn't try to prompt him to address this person or any other. He merely talked to the people there and regularly such people were completely free to talk to whoever people they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you've answered this question. Just a small precision you can easily answer. Were you always present when the witnesses talked to refugees or displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was frequently present; however, I needed rest from time to time, whereby I would withdraw and leave my guests to talk to the displaced persons or refugees, especially if there was an interpreter in attendance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you have said that either you went or Mr. Granic went and perhaps you went not all alone. When you couldn't go with them, would some deputy of yours accompany them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to make sure, because you indicated that at times when you weren't there, you needed some rest, and you would withdraw and allow your guests. Now, was it then when you would withdraw that they were accompanied by somebody as well? In other words, were they free by themselves or did they always have a chaperon?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases when some of those visitors expressly stated, This is where I want to be left alone, and then I would withdraw and there were cases like that. And they would usually stay there with an interpreter and they would usually bring an interpreter of their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you a follow-up question about something that is very important in this case. We've seen pictures, videos, of people who were detained for days or months on end. And when they left these sites some of these people had lost 10 to 20 kilos, some people had lost a lot of weight. Afterwards, these people went to Croatia as refugees. Do you remember receiving that type of persons, people, who had lost a lot of weight, who were sick? Do you remember them telling you their stories? Did they have access to the media, to the UNHCR, to foreign officials, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received such people as well. If possible, if they could stay in a displaced persons or refugee centre, they would receive all necessary supplies and health care. If such people were coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were so exhausted that they couldn't stay in a refugee centre, they would be hospitalised for a short period of time. Of course hospital care was free of charge for displaced persons as well as refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you were made aware of some cases of this type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of some such cases, especially when it comes to persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the occupied part of Croatia. They came without any possessions of their own, save for a plastic bag, and even that would frequently be taken away from them when moving from the occupied territory into the free territory. Those on the other side would do that. There were numerous violations of human rights in such instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could move rather quickly now with the next set of documents, 1D 02586, we see your name at the bottom again with somebody else's signature. Again, can you confirm that this was a document that you would have seen at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document. It was drafted in late November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to the next one, 1D 02613 is a very similar document, as is 1D 02614, 2612, 2611, if you can -- and then 2615. These are all 1D 0 documents. If you could look at all of those, and could you please tell us whether these are the documents -- these documents were generated by your office and whether you were familiar with them at the time they were drafted.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, looking at the documents before me, I can tell you that I knew of them during the time I worked in the office. These were regular reports aimed at the public and the media. The media kept asking data from us. This concerns April 1994, October 1994, December 1994. Your Honours, one can conclude from that that basically every month we informed the public about the situation concerning displaced persons and refugees. Our public was interested in that. We tried to raise the level of sensitivity of our public so as to contribute in terms of money and food and so that we could accommodate displaced persons and refugees in a better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at another very large document, this is a report, and it's 3D 01030, it's 3D 01030. And I'm going to ask you if you could just look through it and see whether you recognise it and whether you recognise the content in this document and how so. The usher will help you, sir. It's 3D 01030. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] I've found it. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with refugees who had been driven out of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, which lasted between 1991 and 1995. It is a detailed report that can be used by anyone who had any interest in it in order to acquaint themselves with the refugee and displaced persons situation in the Republic of Croatia. It is a rather lengthy document with detailed information on all refugees and displaced persons as well as individual locations, such as Velika Kladusa and Kupljensko which represented a separate problem in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know who generated this document; and if so, how is it that you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document came out of the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees as well. It was drafted by the department of information --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could stop you there. Let me show you the first page which is in B/C/S. If I could have the usher's attention here to help us out. The first -- it's -- the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't have it. It's not in English, but you have it, it's just very difficult to find. If you could just look at that. This is the first page to the document in the original language.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. This is not our office's document, judging by the cover page, which is of course very important. It can tell you something more about who put that data together. That data is probably based upon the information provided by our office to the public and to the media as well as to other humanitarian organizations. But the report as such was not drafted by our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell from looking at the front page who drafted the report?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see here that it was done by Mr. Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- excuse me, let me just -- I'm going to lead you through this. Did General Praljak ever come to you asking for archival material in order to put this report together?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Slobodan Praljak came to me after having called me by telephone. We talked and he asked me to give him any documents I might have on the activities of our office in terms of data and numbers. I told him I had such documents and that I was willing to hand them over that day. He sent another person to my office to whom I handed over many files and documents. It was a pile this high. Mr. Praljak studied all the papers I had given him, and they were only a part of the large archives we had at our office, and I mostly gave him copies. I told Mr. Praljak to go to the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees where in addition to the papers I had given him he can find much more data. Mr. Praljak did, indeed, go to the office and I asked the head to provide him with the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. There may be an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Once again, Your Honour, if we could first of all, number one, get a date for when these conversations with Mr. Praljak occurred. I'll start with that and then I have a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could -- I haven't left the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me then, if that's the case, Mr. Karnavas, let me continue to respond to what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if you haven't left the topic, ask the witness to tell you on what day Mr. Praljak came because that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there are a series of other questions that I was about to ask and I'm getting interrupted. It seems a bit premature. But let's hear the rest of the objection so maybe I can deal with all of them at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it appears to me, Your Honour, and based on this situation I'm acting, admittedly, since we don't have any data information -- haven't been provided data information, but I'm required at this point to engage in a certain amount of conjecture, which I prefer not to do, if we could just simply get a date. But it appears to me likely just looking at some of the material this is a document which was prepared by Mr. Praljak specifically for the purposes of this litigation. It's his own self-serving expert report, apparently, that's what it looks like; if I'm wrong, I'll be corrected, that's what it looks like. And I would object to the examination of it -- of the witness. If Mr. Praljak wants to take the stand and defend his own work and be subject to cross-examination, then that might be one way to do it; but for Mr. Praljak to create a self-serving "expert report" and then have this witness opine about it I think is objectionable. And that's our objection, and my question about the timing stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just to -- first of all, the document has already been admitted, that's number 1. Number two, as far as I understand it has been admitted on previous occasions or at least it's been referenced. Number two, the question is whether the gentleman who generated this particular document came and got certain information that is now in the document itself. Now, we have Dr. Rebic, who indicated at one point General Praljak came to him and asked for archival material. So I don't know whether General Praljak is going to testify and whether he's going to go into this report. I'm merely asking this particular gentleman because there's a follow-up question in addition to this report, which I'll get to in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Dr. Rebic, do you recall about what time was it, what period was it, that Dr. -- that General Praljak came to see you, asking for documents so he could prepare the report that -- or the book that he prepared? Do you recall a year?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I cannot recall the year because a lot of time has passed. It could have been four or six years ago, but I can't tell you any precise dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there are two photographs in this report. Maybe we can put them on the ELMO. The ERN number is 3D 260191 and 192, 191 and 192. If you could page through the report and we can put this on the ELMO, it may be quicker for everyone unless you have it on the e-court. I'm labouring under severe time pressures. Okay. Now, do you recognise -- this should be on the screen. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I do have the photo on the screen and before me in the binder. These are the archives of our Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of documents contained in there, a lot of data, all the first names and family names of all the refugees and displaced persons who have ever been registered in our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at the next document which would be 3D 0260192, that's the very next page, we'll see another photograph. Now, it's on the screen. Now, do you see this? Do you recognise what's in this photo?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it. Again, this is the same place, the archives of the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons. This place is really huge. A few people could spend a lot of time, years maybe, in studying the situation that we had with refugees and displaced persons in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, indeed you indicate in your report, the report that you made yesterday, Dr. Rebic, if I could get your attention. Don't worry about the binder, sir, don't worry about it. I just want to -- in your report, in your report that we went through yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you kindly assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday we looked at your report, 1D 02921. We don't need to look at it, but on page 25 it does indicate that early September you received a delegation from ICTY in The Hague, and this would have been September 1994. And you describe a Mr. Antonius Kempenaars, head of the delegation, and you gave them all the data the office disposed of. Is that correct, sir, that as early as 1994 the ICTY had a delegation which had access to all of this data of which you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, in light of the -- and I'm going into another topic, it might be good if we can take a break at this point, otherwise I can go on. It doesn't matter to me. I can go on for another ten minutes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, while we're at a pause then, on the last document that we were talking about before, and I didn't want to interrupt before Mr. Karnavas was finished with that document, I'm referring for the record 3D 01030, our record -- just so the record is clear, our records show that there were three pages, three individual pages of that document which appear to have been admitted to date. 3D 26-0211, 3D 26-0256, and 3D 26-0258. The date information that we've been provided - and all I can say is that's what we've been provided - was the document was created on the 15th of June, 2007. So since -- in the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was by the Prosecutor, and I don't want to get into a situation where we're debating points here, was when General Praljak visited the gentleman, that's what started all of this. It's going to be up to the Trial Chamber, which we're constantly reminded by our professional Judges who can decipher through all of this, what to make of this particular resort. The purpose of the questioning was, one, we went through a series of reports. What I'm trying to demonstrate here is that, one, there was total transparency. Two, there you have a documented archive that was available to everyone, including the ICTY, the Prosecution had access to all of this as early as 1994, and perhaps had they looked through these documents part of the indictment would have been written slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially with respect to their representation of what the Republic of Croatia was doing with the refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to spend hours on this. Witness, you said it yourself, the OTP went in 1994, and you said that they could access all the documents. Here's my question: Did Mr. Praljak come after or before the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's no good reason for Mr. Karnavas's argument. I simply was trying to assist the Chamber and provide the Chamber with as much information as possible. I've asked for date information repeatedly. I don't think there's anything improper about that, and I just simply -- and the representation was also made about admission, and I simply wanted to provide the Chamber with as much information as possible as to the three pages that had previously been admitted and with the date associated with the document which is according -- as far as we can tell was June 2007, which does tend to confirm what I indicated to the Chamber was my belief a few minutes ago; and that is, this is a document that was apparently prepared by Mr. Praljak for the purposes of this litigation. And I just want the record to reflect that. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, since you've been named, what do you have to say? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] A distinction should be made between the time when the document was compiled and when it was issued. Those are two different times. There's one time when the document was compiled and another time when the publisher found the funds to actually publish it and put it on the market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Prosecution continues to engage in these sorts of tactics, I do reserve the right to also engage in these tactics as well. I know how to be combative in court. I don't want to give the impression that simply because I'm being rather kind and comforting to the Prosecutor today that I will continue to be -- to do so in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next set of documents. Now, if we could go to 1D 02587, 2587, and if you could look at this document and there's a series of documents that we will be going through, basically it's the same topic, the topic as we will see deals with guarantees. This one -- I'm sorry, this one deals with the financing, this set of topics. Are you familiar with Mr. Jozo Martinovic? I believe he's passed away since.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm familiar with Mr. Jozo Martinovic. He was the minister of finance at the time when I was appointed the head of the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And since he was involved with finances, we had a lot of contacts; and yes, you're right, in the meantime he has died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a question -- do you recognise, first of all, this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the document. This was the Crisis Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina which received $30 million US from the Republic of Croatia to urgently deal with the issue of the numerous refugees and for humanitarian purposes, to help people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you know - because this question came up last week - whether this was a loan to be paid back or was this a gift?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know and according to what I remember, this was a gift which was never repaid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could look at very quickly 1D 02606, and we've gone through this last week so we don't need a lot of discussion on this. But do you recognise this document; and if so, what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this document. This is about the purchase of oil stores that we bought for our refugee centres which did not have any other forms of heating. Those were mainly places on the coast or the places or former military centres or barracks without any systematic source of heating, and we had to provide something because we had constant objections from the refugees who were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, 1D 02608, and then let's look at this very quickly. We see at the second page, we see your name and we see where this information was sent to. The subject matter is: "One-time financial assistance to hosts of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina." Could you please explain to us exactly what was this document for and how was it used?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this document was a one-off financial aid to the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina and families that accommodated them. This type of assistance was provided on several occasions. I sent this report to Dr. Mate Granic, the Deputy Prime Minister, who was in charge of all social issues, as well as to the minister of labour and social welfare because this ministry was in charge of the social welfare of all our citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next document 1D 02607, we see again the subject matter: "One-time financial assistance for refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who organized their lives independently and for their hosts." And again we see your name at the end or the second page. This is a similar document which covers basically the same sort of costs as you've indicated; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is another one-time financial assistance which was given in February 1993 to the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina who organized their life independently or were accommodated with families, which points to the fact that many -- the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina were accommodated with Croatian citizens and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02778, we saw this last week but if you could look at this again and please tell us if you recognise this document and tell us who generated it.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here the Government of the Republic of Croatia, Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, which points to the fact clearly that this document was issued by our office. I recognise this document because this was a letter that we dispatched from our office to our general public, appealing to the citizens to help as much as they could in food, in money that would go towards the care of our displaced persons and refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the way I tried to appeal for the solidarity of our citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 026 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas, we may as well take the break now, it's quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. This would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have a break. In terms of time, I believe you have another hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, very very quickly, very quickly, we're going to go through some documents because we need to get to the second binder -- or my next binder, but the next document is 1D 02625, 2625. Over here this document -- first of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 625 [In English] Government of the Republic of Croatia [Interpretation] I recognise the document. This was compiled by the government and it was sent to the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry Of Tourism, and the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons. This document was compiled by the government in order to define how much the office should pay for the care of refugees and displaced persons in different types of accommodation, including hotels and others. This sets the price per person at 6.7 German marks for a whole day board and lodging in the hotel and this is further broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look to the next document -- I don't mean to rush you, sir, but just -- we're under tremendous time pressures here, 2589. We see your name at the bottom. Do you recognise this document and very briefly what is this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the document. This is my authentic signature. This is payment of financial reimbursement, refugees from Vojvodina and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were given that reimbursement for temporary use, and the same went for the assets provided to them by the Government of the Republic of Croatia, they were also for their temporary use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next set of documents relate to some documents that were either generated for or came from the internationals. The first one is 1D 02609. If we look at the second page we see your signature and we see the date, 3 February 1993. It says here this is a letter of mutual intent to conclude an agreement, this is with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and we see that it has been signed on their behalf by Mr. Jacques Mouchet. Did you know Mr. Mouchet?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I know Mr. Jacques Mouchet very well indeed. He was the head of the UNHCR mission in 1993. I had a very close cooperation with him. Together we dealt with the problems that arose, especially when it came to the care for refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. As you have rightly told us, this document is an agreement or a letter of understanding as to how we would distribute the $30 million that the UNHCR provided for refugees and displaced persons. This was assistance to the families that looked after the refugees and displaced persons and also other programmes that need not be mentioned in any particular details because all the details are provided herein. So whoever is interested in learning about them may avail themselves of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just inquire for a clarification. We had a document where $30 million, exactly the same sum here, was promised by the Croatian government to the ODPR. I would assume it is something entirely different as compared to this sum, but maybe you can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two things at stake. The 30 million that we mentioned just a while ago was a gift by the Croatian government to the Crisis Staff which was supposed to help the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the very beginning of the war in dealing with some very important issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The other 30 million is the money that we received from UNHCR as assistance for various programmes, one of them being helping families who cared for the refugees and other programmes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but that's quite enough. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, you will have noticed that the first document that you made reference to which is 1D 02587, the date is May 13th, 1992, whereas this one is in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to -- August of 1993. It's February, I'm sorry, February 1993. Now, if we could go to the next document, 1D 02592, and we look at the second page of this document we see your signature, and this is addressed to Mr. Mouchet. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the document. It was signed by myself. The signature is absolutely authentic. This is a letter that I wrote to Mr. Jacques Mouchet with regard to the humanitarian aid to Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina which was provided at the request of Cardinal Vinko Puljic, the Archbishop of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document 1D 02605, 2605, we see your name at the bottom, we see your signature, and yesterday you did mention VIP company and a Mr. Binenfeld, you mentioned that individual, Binenfeld. Thank you. Now, could you -- do you recognise this document and what is -- what are we talking about in this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I recognise this document. The document mentions a sum of money which was spent on the census of refugees and displaced persons in 1994 and for the computer data analysis. The sum in question is 404.000 USD plus 20.000 USD. This is the money which was spent for the registration of the refugees and displaced persons, and this is a sort of confirmation that I received the money from UNHCR and spent it for the given purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document is 1D 02604, it's dated June 1, 1994. We see your signature at the bottom with your name. This is again addressed to Mr. Mouchet. Again, all of this is for confirmation to the Trial Chamber as far as your cooperation with UNHCR. Can you please tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a letter that I sent to UNHCR, to Mr. Jacques Mouchet, regarding the financial assistance that was provided to our office in October 1993. The money that was left over, which was originally intended for 1994, we asked them to be able to spend it in 1993 because we had huge expenses and outlays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at 1D 02603, now, this is dated June 7th, 1994. Again we see your signature and we see a second signature as well, and this is again addressed to Mr. Mouchet. This is a similar document, is it not, to the one that we just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a similar document to the one that we've just discussed, I signed it myself, and the co-signatory was Dr. Maja Kurent, and who was in charge of cooperation with international humanitarian organizations. She was as -- our minister of foreign affairs, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And now the last document related to this particular topic is 1D 02602, 2602. This is September 27, 1994, again we see your name at the bottom, we see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for everyone's attention, on paragraph number 2 it talks about, "The Republic of Croatia has become entirely exhausted through the long-lasting care of refugees and DPs, and is unfortunately no longer able to cover the refugees' organized accommodation costs." Then if we skip a paragraph we see that there is a summary with respect to some camps, some centres and a hotel, but we also see -- I want to draw everyone's attention to Obonjan and Gasinci. And if we look at the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just look at this and please tell us what this is because these are -- those two particular centres have been mentioned by a Ms. Azra Krajsek as being troublesome centres where the Muslims were apparently not being treated in a very favourable manner. So can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the issue of whether the treatment was equal for everyone, the treatment of refugees and displaced persons was more or less the same. However, there were instances in which displaced persons were accommodated in a better way or sometimes in a worse way than refugees. It is difficult, however, to say something for each of the refugee centres individually. However, you can see here as regards Obonjan that in the first seven months of 1994, $345.000 USD were spent. As regards Gasinci, during this same period, the first half of 1994, $3 million and almost $500.000 USD were spent. You can see from there that Gasinci was the most expensive centre to maintain. We wanted the refugees there to be taken care of in as good way as possible under the circumstances. Then we see all the other centres which housed refugees as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the purpose of that document was to show the transparency involved. Now, if you flip the page you'll see there's another document, and it is not numbered but by accident it was attached to this, and this is dated September 6th, 1994. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask a little complementary question to the previous list. Can you give us indications, sir, on the number of refugees and displaced persons that were accommodated in Gasinci and Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment I cannot remember any precise figures, therefore I will approximate. In Gasinci at the time the figure was around 4.000 refugees, up to 4 and a half thousand. In Obonjan there were less. On the island at the time there were between 2 and 2 and a half thousand refugees. I don't think we ever exceeded that number; however, at times there were less refugees. This is a -- sort of a general piece of information that I can recall off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And attached to this document is another document which is rather separate and probably deserves a separate number but it's been attached to it. And I just want confirmation, this is September 6th, 1994. We see your name but we don't see a signature under your name. We do see a signature for a Dr. Maja Kurent, but it looks like somebody signed for this individual. Do you recognise this document? It's the last -- yes, yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the document. I did not sign it, however, it was signed by Maja Kurent, who is a physician by profession, and she would usually sign Dr., D-r, although she held a master's degree in medical science. She had the right to sign documents on my behalf concerning UNHCR issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine. All right. Now we're going to switch to another topic and we probably need to get you the next binder, if you could be assisted, and we're going to focus on something different. The document that we're going to be -- that I will refer you to is P 00336. We see this document, it's a Prosecution document, commonly referred to as a presidential transcript, it's 21 July 1992. And it would appear, if question go to page 3 of this document, which is 3 of 184 pages, that you would have been present there, your name being mentioned, Dr. Rebic, chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian -- I mean secretary of the Office for Refugees, Dr. Rebic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see my name there, and I recall the discussion which took place on that occasion and I also remember the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't want to go into the substance because we can all read this and we've had other witnesses, but very briefly if you could tell us if you remember the occasion and if you can give us an impression of what transpired, what was the atmosphere like during this rather lengthy discussion of 184 pages?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it was a meeting between a Croatian governmental delegation headed by the president of the republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and a Bosnia-Herzegovina delegation headed by Dr. Izetbegovic. The meeting was held on the 21st of July, 1992, in the office of the president. I remember it was a very long discussion, it lasted from noon until 10.00 p.m. that day. In my view, it was a very open discussion. The people involved expressed their views, expressed their concerns and problems, the Croatian side to the Bosnian side and the other way around. They were being honest and they tried to deal with very serious issues, that is, the responsibility of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the defence of their homeland of Bosnia-Herzegovina. President Tudjman had a firm position that Bosnia-Herzegovina needs to remain as a whole country with three constituent peoples and that the relations among them should be arranged. He invited Izetbegovic, as the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to do his utmost so that in those difficult wartime conditions that war in Bosnia-Herzegovina be finished as soon as possible, through joint cooperation of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. On the Croatian side what was promised was assistance to the extent to that the Republic of Croatia as an independent country could provide to another independent country, this being Bosnia-Herzegovina. Occasionally tension rose since the topics discussed were very important ones; however, the discussion would always be calmed down and it resulted in a document being signed by Dr. Franjo Tudjman on the Croatian side and Mr. Izetbegovic on the Bosnia-Herzegovinian side. It was called document on friendship and cooperation of two sovereign states in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. And if I can just -- and just for the record I believe on page 43, line 9, Dr. Rebic said the Bosnian and Herzegovinian side, as opposed to the Bosnian side. In any event, if we look at the next document which is P 00339, P 00339, it's a Prosecution document, we've seen it before, and you've just mentioned that an agreement was signed and indeed we have this dated 21 July 1992. And if I could just focus your attention to paragraph number 3. Okay. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Where it talks -- we can see the state delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina expresses their gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for having received and provided for refugees -- have you found that passage?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, it is item 3 [In English] "Bosnia-Herzegovina express their gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for having received and provided for refugees from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina beyond the capacity of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Now if -- we don't need to read the entire next paragraph, but if you look at the last sentence of the next paragraph, it talks about a separate protocol on cooperation will be signed for the purpose," and it talks of -- and if we read the entire paragraph it talks about the purpose for providing for humanitarian assistance, financial aid, construction of refugee centres. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is what the gist of the document was. I could only wish that all the sides implemented the document in full. The war would have been over much sooner, and when I say "all the sides involved," I mean the third side as well which was the JNA and unfortunately it was not one of the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did the Republic of Croatia carry out on its promise to provide humanitarian assistance, financial aid, and constructing, for instance, refugee centres since you were the head of the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To my knowledge, the Republic of Croatia as regards the construction of refugee centres provided enormous assistance in terms of accommodating refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was the Government of the Republic of Croatia who bore the most expenses. We were greatly helped by the UNHCR, I have to say that, but most of the expenses were paid for by the Government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we saw the last sentence of the second paragraph, of paragraph number 3, which talked about the signing of a protocol. Keeping in mind that this agreement was 21 July 1992. Now, if we could flip to the next document, and we saw this last week, the next document which is 3D 02710, 3D 02710, that's the very next document, and we see a protocol. And if we look at the second page we see that it's signed in Zagreb 22 July 1992, that would be one day later. First of all, do you know who will Jure Pelivan is?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Karnavas. I know who Jure Pelivan is. He was the then-president. He signed it on behalf of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same as Franjo Greguric who signed the document on behalf of the Croatian government.
