I met Mr. Jure Pelivan for the first time in late January 1992, when together with Minister Jurlina I went to Bosnia-Herzegovina to visit our Croatian refugees who were then accommodated in Bosnia-Herzegovina, since by that time we were at war with the JNA. First there was the aggression against Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was still a free country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, together with Jurlina, I was received by President Jure Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this protocol, if we look at it, can you tell us whether it relates to the protocol that's being referenced in the agreement that was signed one day earlier in Zagreb as part of the Friendship and Cooperation Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a part of the document on friendship and cooperation. That document was supposed to be signed by both governments in order for the document to be legally valid and so that it could be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to point 4 very briefly which is on page 2, and it reads: "The Government of the Republic of Croatia and the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall request more humanitarian aid from international community, especially for Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as reception in neighbouring European countries of new refugees, who will not be taken care of in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Government of the Republic of Croatia is not able to cover the costs of transportation of international humanitarian aid, which is sent directly to Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, does this accurately reflect the situation as it was back then?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it does reflect the situation precisely as it was at the time and as it was about to become. Bosnia and Herzegovina, together with the Republic of Croatia, agreed on Croatia assisting in terms of accommodation for the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since Croatia expressed its concern that it would not be able to cover all the expenses involved, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia agreed to send out an appeal to other countries to assist not only in terms of humanitarian aid, that is, food, but also to receive some refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Such reception of Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees in cooperation with the UNHCR was in keeping with the document on cooperation and friendship which had been signed so that the refugees could be sent onwards to other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, were they supposed to take some of the refugees or all of the refugees? We're talking about these European countries with the assistance of UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only some countries because most of the countries did not even respond to the appeal for help. Those that did in cooperation with the UNHCR received a smaller number of Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees who went via Croatia on to third countries or after some time in Croatia would leave for another country. It was a rather small number whilst most of them remained in Croatia, where they were taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go through a series of other documents that are related somewhat to what we just talked about. The next document is 1D 02008, 2008. We see it's dated 21 November 1992, and if you just look through this document, please tell us whether you know anything about what's contained in this document. We know that your document was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We all are, Your Honour, we all are, trust me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- we see that Mate Granic attended a particular meeting. Can you please tell us whether you recognise this document, what's contained inside the document.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the contents of the document, and the information of Mate Granic when he returned from the meeting in Bosnia-Herzegovina where he visited Grude to meet some representatives of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian government as well as local Croatian authorities. The discussion they held concerned the problems which came about towards the end of 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Republic of Croatia was asked to assist in resolving those problems. More or less, that is all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's focus on some of these paragraphs, and first I'm going to go to paragraph number 6. It says here: "At the request of Herceg-Bosna, it is necessary to resolve as soon as possible the issue of military conscripts located in Croatia and prevent the citizens of Herceg-Bosna from becoming employed in Croatia." Can you comment on this? Why was it necessary?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know well that we in the Republic of Croatia concerning the displaced persons who were male of military age, we tried to persuade them to take part in the defence of the country. Most men between 20 and 40 years of age were at the front lines in Croatia defending their country. It was only understandable that Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say not only Herceg-Bosna but also the Bosnian Muslim side, occasionally asked the Republic of Croatia to help in returning such males who can take part in the defence. It was also asked from us on occasion by the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a matter of cooperation and friendship between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the events that followed, I did not come across any significant problems, and the office as such was not involved in it. As the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, we abided by the instructions and we worked within the framework of the Geneva Conventions pertaining to the accommodation of displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'm going to have to ask you to have shorter answers because we've covered a lot of this in the narrative yesterday. Very briefly, if we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry for interrupting you. I would like to ask a question from Dr. -- from our witness that -- concerning paragraph 1 and paragraph 1 of this letter, and other kind of [indiscernible] of the talks. And here we can read that, and I quote: "In connection with refugees, it was stressed that Croatia does not have the physical, social, or material capabilities to receive a new wave of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina that is expected." And then it continues: "The only possibility is transit to other countries." Now my question is, Dr. Rebic, is the following: First of all, to which street -- or which kind of people refers to in that very much in that paragraph, is it only about, let's say men or those who are likely to also discussed a few minutes ago in paragraph 6, that is the military conscripts, et cetera, or does it mean a general confirmation or acceptance that no more refugees could be allowed to go to Croatia and because there was no physical possibilities to take them as far as the scarcity of the resources? And it is number one question. The number two question is that: What kind of measures, if any, were taken to make a possibility of a transit of those persons to other countries, and if you have some numerical way of telling us how many people in that epoch in 1992, late 1992 and early 1993, were transferred or allowed to leave Croatia for some other countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me tell you that I was not present during that meeting, so I can only speak from my memory and based on what was confirmed by this document. It is true that Granic asked from the Bosnian and Herzegovinian side to take more involvement in the accommodation of their displaced persons instead of sending them all to the Republic of Croatia, whose resources had already been exhausted at the moment. When you ask me about the number, I can tell you that at that moment there were approximately 250.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina residing in Croatia. That's why attempts were made to talk to people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in this particular case in Herzegovina, because talks were with Dr. Jadranko Prlic to establish a similar office to the one in Croatia that would be in charge within the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina of displaced persons instead of dispatching them all to Croatia or third countries. As far as the number of people who were sent to us -- who were sent to third countries at that time, I must say that it was not on a very large scale. This only started in the course of 1993 when the number of those refugees who were sent to third countries [as interpreted] from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina surpassed all our abilities. We were talking yesterday about the numbers in comparison between the number of refugees and the population of Croatia, and I believe that you understood the scope of the problem. And that's why Prlic was asked -- or Prlic offered or asked Granic himself to help with the work of such an office, and this was also done for the Bosniak Muslim side. At that time, Mrs. Omersoftic arrived in Sarajevo -- from Sarajevo in my office in Zagreb and asked me to give her detailed instruction as to how an office of that sort could be established. Mrs. Omersoftic from Sarajevo was provided with very detailed instructions as to how to care for refugees and displaced persons. In a nutshell attempts were made to help Bosnia and Herzegovina to look after its own displaced persons wherever it could, wherever the area was threat-free, and there were such areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One point to clarify on page 51, line 8, it should say -- it was referring to 1993 when the refugees in Croatia were sent to third countries, so "in Croatia" was not in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But just following up on the question that was asked by Judge Prandler we see that this is 20 November 1992, and if I could get you to reflect back then --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and tell us whether the hotels where the refugees were being accommodated at and displaced persons, especially at the Adriatic, whether they were capable at the time of having such refugees there during the winter months.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm saying in -- we're back to 20 November 1992. Dr. Prlic is meeting with Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to paragraph number 1, we see that the Republic of Croatia is stressed and we saw documents concerning heaters and what have you.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, some of us haven't been to the Adriatic coast, some of us have. At that period of time, would those facilities that were being used to house refugees and displaced persons, did they have the capabilities, the facilities, for winter accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have capabilities for winter accommodation. The hotels and workers' holiday resorts were primarily intended for tourists and citizens of Croatia for summer vacation. It was very difficult to keep these people in such hotels in winter-time. November is the time when winter starts, but I will say just briefly that the situation was analogous to Croatia. At the time Croatia was largely occupied and cared for its own displaced persons. It was supposed at the time that Bosnia and Herzegovina could do the same, although it was occupied in large parts of its territories there is still free territories where it could care for its displaced persons and the actions went along that channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just -- and then briefly one more paragraph to focus on because we have to move along. Paragraph number 5, it says: "Full coordination should be effected concerning the status of refugees from Herceg-Bosna. Inform the Herceg-Bosna HVO of the underlying ideas behind the suggested protocols between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to the education of refugees, health protection, and opening logistical centres for humanitarian aid." Now, could you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the letter of understanding signed between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as based on the international laws on looking after refugees and displaced persons, Croatia took a commitment to provide refugees with education, health care, and that it will provide Bosnia and Herzegovina with logistical centres for humanitarian aid, and these centres were indeed organized in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. If we go to the next document, 1D 02283. Now we're into 25 February 1993, we're moving in a chronological order, starting with the meeting that was had, the friendship agreement, the protocol. Now we see here 25 February 1993, we see another protocol and this is for the establishment of logistic centres in the Republic of Croatia for the reception and distribution of humanitarian aid sent to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you aware of this protocol, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of this protocol, and I also knew that within that protocol in Croatia we ensured the logistical support for humanitarian aid. There were logistical centres of that kind in Croatia, and from there help was sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Bosnia-Herzegovina was helped with the humanitarian aid from those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if we go to another document, this is 2D 00454, 2D 00454. The issue of transfers to third countries and guarantees has come up at some point. If we could look at this particular document, it's dated Sarajevo, April 7, 1993. If we look at the last -- the second page, we see who signed it, Smajic --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hajrudin Smajic signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And we also see at the very top of the very first page, it's UNPROFOR at Sarajevo for communications officer HVO. Subject: "Request for safe exit from Sarajevo." Now, if we could look at -- unfortunately we don't have too much time to dwell on this too much, but look at the third paragraph on the first page, and it says and I'll read it slowly: "Most of these individuals are travelling towards Split and they are all in possession of individual guarantees from other countries that they are going to be taken care of within those countries. Some individuals are leaving for other parts of Republic of BiH and they are not going to leave BiH, and from the lists you can determine that among individuals to be evacuated there is a major number of Croatian citizens, as well as individuals with necessary guarantees from the Republic of Croatia." Now, attached to this we see that there is a list, and it would appear that the list is rather extensive.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 108 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, if you look at the list you will see -- my colleague tells me here that it's approximately 1.200 people, but we could be wrong. But in any event, could you please tell us a little bit about this, about letters of guarantee and what have you. Did your office have anything to do with issuing letters of guarantee for citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to go to third countries through Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it came to transfer to third countries through Croatia, our office could not issue any papers. What our office could do and could provide the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina with was the so-called entry visa, but this was not a visa in the legal sense of the word. It was just a piece of paper issued by our office to people from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who could use that piece of paper if they didn't have a passport or any other document, to enter the Republic of Croatia and the police had to let them cross the border because they were obviously enjoying some sort of a refugee status and the Republic of Croatia guaranteed that they would provide them with the proper refugee status. At that time those were usually people of Croatian ethnicity who had relatives in Croatia or friends in Croatia. You have to know that a lot of citizens of Croatia, of the Republic of Croatia, originated from Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the end of the day, I originate from one such family that had to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina 200 years ago, and that's why I dare say that one-third of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia hail from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a result the 200-years-old ethnic cleansing of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, I want to focus you on the topic that we're dealing with, and I'm going to ask you to please just answer my questions directly. And then if the Court wishes or anyone else wishes for additional information, they can do so. But with respect to this list, if you look at this list, on this -- from looking at the names, are we looking at Croats? Are we looking at Muslims? Are we looking at both? Can you just take a look at some of the names.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- you don't have to give me the names just tell me, does this list have both Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the list has both Croats and Muslims. There are Ismets, Zeljkos, Marijas, Samiras, Lejlas, and Fadilas. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document P 10048, this is dated 16 July 1993. We see your name. If we look at the Croatian version, it doesn't appear, at least from the naked eye, it doesn't appear to be your signature. Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly whose signature it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. By looking at this document can you help us because it says here on the subject: "Approval for entry and temporary stay in Republic Croatia." There is a list of 500 persons who will be temporarily accommodating in Gasinci centre in Djakovo. To your knowledge, is this an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from what I see, this should be an authentic document. Such documents were issued at request of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina to allow them to cross the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia without any problems. As you can see, this document was sent to the police station in Vrgorac, to the border police, and to the border crossing in Banja Luka. In other words, the police, the Croatian police, had to have a document from our office at the border in order to allow them to cross the border and to be sure that the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons guaranteed to provide them with care and that the office would bear the cost of their living if they remained in Croatia or if they left for third countries then it would be some third country who would bear the expenses of their stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So once they came in, they would be your responsibility, your office's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me return to this document, it's a document of some importance. According to this document, 500 persons from Mostar will not enjoy refugee status. They will have to leave for a third country. Furthermore, these persons will be on board buses and will be escorted by the police. How long did it take you to process 500 files, the 500 files of these persons? The date is the 16th of July 1993. What would have prevented Mostar resident coming to Croatia from applying for refugee status? Something that is completely impossible according to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, those were people who I suppose had a previous agreement with UNHCR, which at that time was involved in the care for Bosnian refugees in third countries. What these persons had asked for was to spend some time in the Republic of Croatia, and this was done. These persons guaranteed that they would proceed travelling towards third countries. Based on that, these persons were provided with temporary accommodation in Gasinci near Djakovo and in some other centres, because a number like that could not have been accommodated in Gasinci alone. And some of them obviously found accommodation with friends and family, and then after a certain while they would ask UNHCR or some other international organization or embassy to provide them with documents to go to a third country and ask for temporary accommodation there. Most often those were people who had friends or family members in Germany, because a lot of people from Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do not start digressing. The -- this case we are very familiar with it of course. What you're telling us is that these 500 persons were taken care of by the UNHCR, and if I understand correctly you were in charge of logistics. And if I understand correctly, the UNHCR was in charge of the entire operation. What you did was just provide accommodation before these people finally left, but you had absolutely no responsibility when it came to what would happen to them later because that was the remit of the UNHCR and of other countries. Is that the way I should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. As soon as they were taken into our care by our refugee centres, whether they got official papers on their status or not, as soon as these persons were in refugee centres ipso facto they were in our care. For as long as they stayed in the Republic of Croatia the Republic of Croatia had to look after them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please do not stray; my question was very specific. We have a document here that shows that 500 persons from Mostar are going to leave for third countries --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes and no, it all depended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this document establishes that these persons will not obtain refugee status; that's what we can read in the third paragraph of the document. You have told us that all this was happening under the control of the UNHCR that took care of the reception in third countries, of letters of guarantee, and so on and so forth. I'm quite ready to accept your explanation, but that would mean that your office only has a logistical role to play, your only function is to accommodate these refugees for a short period of time. That's an interpretation, a possible interpretation, of this document. But if we assume that the UNHCR does not play any role because these 500 persons have managed to go to a third country of their own accord, and if the UNHCR does not play any role here, then I wonder about the role played by the ODPR because you are supposed to be in charge of refugees and apparently you were not ready to grant refugee status to these persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the assumptions that you have just presented, although I myself did not write that letter, but I assume that based on that letter the office was also supposed to take these people in its care. But again - and I assume again because I was not privy to any such case, I know that there were such cases - those were people who already at the border stated that they wanted to proceed towards third countries and that they only asked for temporary stay in Croatia. Based on that statement they were offered temporary accommodation in the Republic of Croatia. If it so happened that such persons stayed in Croatia longer or permanently - and there were such cases - then the office would issue them with a certificate on the refugee status that they would then enjoy. There were such cases. In other words, I would say that this is more an anomaly than a rule and it could not be used to draw a conclusion that the Office of Refugees refused to take in such persons only because those people had stated for various reasons that they want to proceed towards third countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we have 500 persons coming from Mostar. It's an important event and that should have caught your attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it caught your attention. But now we find that these 500 persons have only received an authorisation for entry and temporary stay in Croatia; in other words, these persons are not going to stay in Croatia. It's obvious, and you stress that by adding that they will not obtain refugee status -- although some of these people may have wanted to remain in Croatia, some of them may not have wanted to go to Hungary, Switzerland, or another country. That's the reason why I wonder about the actual role of your office. Were you just a tool used to make sure that these people carried on to other countries, or were you just charged with accommodating them for a short period of time, because the entire thing was not your problem, it was the problem of UNHCR. That's what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only because it was only UNHCR's problem, it was also a problem of the Republic of Croatia. Those people who arrived from Bosnia and Herzegovina, if they didn't want to receive the status of refugee in the Republic of Croatia but rather stated that they wanted to proceed towards third countries, then such persons - and there were many such cases, this is not the only one - those persons were issued with a temporary refugee status and they could then remain in the Republic of Croatia until they left for third countries. In other words, they themselves wanted to leave. They themselves did not want to receive full refugee status. They only wanted to receive temporary refugee status and for Croatia to be their point of transit on their route to third countries. Croatia could not refuse anybody the right to use it as a transit country. It was a transit country for all the refugees en route to third countries. One should not, therefore, draw a conclusion that the office did not want to take these persons in. If these persons had stated that they wanted to leave for third countries, that they didn't want a permanent refugee status, then these persons did not have the right to ask for a permanent refugee status. It would be a deceit on the part of these persons, if they received such false status. I believe I was clear. We had to respect the rights of those refugees. We could not force them to stay if they didn't wish to do so; we had to rather allow them and help them in their intention to proceed towards third countries. Croatia could not expel refugees to another country because simply enough no other country would receive them. So Croatia had an obligation imposed on it by third countries. So one can only assume that these persons really did not want to stay in Croatia any longer time. They wanted to use Croatia as a point of transit en route to a third country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. If a Muslim resident from Mostar had arrived at the border without any guarantee, without anything, and if he had requested under the Geneva Conventions to obtain refugee status, then what would have happened at the office, at the ODPR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the person wanted to accept refugee status in the Republic of Croatia, that person would have been given that status by the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I add a question. Mr. Rebic, we have seen the documents, the decree and laws on the basis of your office. They state the conditions under which a person is taken in charge by the ODPR. Two categories are mentioned, namely, the displaced persons and refugees. Now, here we have 500 persons who are neither one nor the other. Was there any legal basis on which, nevertheless, you say that your office was in charge of them? Or was that an event extra legum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, and I can repeat, these people, had they wanted to receive the status of refugee in the Republic of Croatia, they would have received it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. That is not at all an answer to my question. My question was: These persons were not refugees. I'm not interested in whether they could have been or not been, and there is another request in that respect too. The question is: Was there a legal basis for your office taking charge of a third category of persons or was it done ad hoc, perhaps out of a warm heart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our office acted within the legal framework. If in this case the people concerned were refugees, they had the right to the status of a refugee. Today I cannot remember exactly whether these were 500 refugees or 500 tourists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Rebic, Mr. Rebic, I have to stop you. I must simply note that you do not want to ask [sic] the question that I put to you but go into another hypothesis. But I leave it at that. I don't want to insist. I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question was to the witness and I don't think counsel should testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not testifying, Your Honour, but obviously you seem to lack a certain understanding. These people, 500 of them, cannot go to Hungary without going through Croatia. They cannot go to Switzerland without going -- they were not flying. So the question is: How do they get to where they want to go. Now, you've assumed some facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Which, could you be more precise? What facts as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That they don't have a status, that they don't have status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It says so expressly in the document, it says they are not refugees and they are certainly not displaced persons, so they are something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I have to go through a country where I have to make a stop and I'm in transit, it appears that they're in transit. Croatia is the transit country. That's what it would appear. But if I'm allowed to continue, but I think that you're assuming that I'm somehow trying to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Is there another objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, the gentleman did try to answer your question, Judge Trechsel, and you interrupted him several times. So there is perhaps something in there that he was trying to explain, albeit maybe he was taking a longer time to get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to point out for the record, Your Honour, there's been a number of references to assumptions just in the last couple of lines of the transcript. Just so the record is clear, the entire last 15 or 20 minutes of the witness's testimony has been based on assumption. This whole thing started out by saying: "Assuming there was an agreement with the UNHCR, assuming, assuming, assuming. We have no basis. He apparently doesn't know, doesn't understand, or doesn't want to answer Judge Trechsel's question, but it's been assumption, assumption, assumption, and no one seems to have picked up on that, but it's gone off on these rabbit trails as if they are facts in evidence and they're not. There is no evidence in the record that there was any agreement with UNHCR, and to assume that UNHCR had any role here is pure assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not suggesting in this particular case. But let me ask this question, Dr. Rebic, and far be it from me to be testifying as I have been accused of by the Bench on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the 500 people here on this list, if all of them had arrived and requested refugee status, whatever the status might have been, travellers, visitors, tourists, if they had come to the border and asked for refugee status, what would you have done? What would the office have done? What would Croatia have done? Please answer this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Office for Displaced Persons of the Republic of Croatia would have given them refugee status. I guarantee that absolutely. Had they asked for refugee status in the Republic of Croatia, they would have received it in the Republic of Croatia. Although, at the time the Republic of Croatia was flooded with refugees. However, we would have come up with means and possibilities to accommodate. However, in this case these people wanted to transit Croatia on their way to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, assuming somebody was coming over land from Bosnia and they wanted to go to, say, Germany or Hungary, which is not too far, given the conditions could they go without going through Croatia? We're talking about going over land, not flying. Because this is important for those of us who don't know the terrain and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In no case could refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina or people from Bosnia-Herzegovina go to third countries without passing through the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Croatia was obliged to grant transit to anyone who wanted to transit through it. If they requested to stay in Croatia for a while, the Office for Displaced Persons enabled them to do so; however, we could not force them to receive refugee status if they did not want that for any reason whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- say that they had secured passage and means to get to any third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday -- again I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, can I finish this line of questioning -- direct examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, very well, very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is in keeping --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've asked for five hours, you've given me four, and now I'm being interrupted. I need to finish this line of thought. I'm being prevented. And then you take the witness in another direction, it makes it virtually impossible for me to focus back. So that's why -- what I'm insisting, I have one more question to this line, I think I should be given deference from the Court. Take as much time as you want, Mr. President, but I think that I'm on my direct examination. There are some accusations that are being lodged at this point; I need to clarify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you will have enough time, do not worry, because of course the time taken by my question will not -- will be deducted from your time. Secondly, what I'm saying is in keeping with what you're saying yourself, and it is also in line with the issue addressed by my fellow Judge earlier on. Witness, let's assume we have someone transiting through your country. In this particular case they were people from Mostar, but they could have been people from China or Poland or could have been anyone. You told us, you explained very clearly, that when you cross a country you need an authorisation. You've travelled the world over. You're very familiar with this, and that's not the problem. The only question the Judges have is the following. What's the role of your office in the transit of these persons? Why is the Ministry of the Interior not taking care of these people? Why isn't it the social affair ministry? Why is the ODPR, an office with a very specific role outlined by legislation, why is the ODPR taking care of these persons? Because these persons were in transit only and they could have been dealt with by other institutions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see how anyone else could have dealt with such great numbers of those people. There was no possibility to accommodate them for short intervals. Only the ODPR had that ability. It was presumed that those people were refugees. They went on to third countries as refugees. They were free to stay in Croatia as refugees, and they would have been given that status as another million of people from Bosnia and Herzegovina had been. One needs to remember how many people from Bosnia-Herzegovina went through the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and we never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you here. You've answered my question. You've told us who else should have taken care of them. I take note of this. Mr. Karnavas, I hope I have not obstructed your examination. My question was a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's assume somebody comes into Croatia and now is declared a refugee. Can you then just deport that person to, say, Slovenia or Hungary or Switzerland? Say, Listen, we have enough, go to Slovenia. Because you told us yesterday of how the Slovenians treated the folks who were at the border for two days and they would not allow them. So could you kindly explain to the Trial Chamber what it was like. Because in order to get to Slovenia you have to go through Croatia, at least during those days by land.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as I said, the Republic of Croatia could not and was not allowed to send anyone to any third countries without papers and agreements, be it directly or through the UNHCR. When refugees are in question, no other neighbouring country wanted to take them from Croatia in case Croatia refused to take them in; it was impossible. Had the 500 wanted to remain in Croatia or had they been unable to transit on to third countries, Croatia would have kept them, would have given them refugee status, and would have taken care of them, irrespective of where they had come from and irrespective of what their status had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go now to the next document, 1D 01710 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D 0170"], because you've made reference of the UNHCR. 1D 01710, and there are a series of documents that I want to go through. This is dated 30 November 1993. We see your name at the bottom, and it says here: "At the request of the Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees, the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees hereby issues its permission for the transit of foreign nationals through the Republic of Croatia. The persons whose names are given in the attached list," and here we have a list of 14, "will be relocated by the UNHCR to the Kingdom of Denmark as part of the family reunification programme."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, just to assist, it is document 1D 01710, and it's not quite correctly in the record here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's 1710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was -- are you familiar with this kind of a document? And I think if you look at it -- if you look at the original one we see your signature or what appears to be your signature.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this is my signature, it is authentic. The text of the request is correct. Upon request by the UNHCR, I provided my agreement for transit of foreign nationals through the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Pursuant to that permission, the UNHCR was able to transit citizens through our territory, otherwise they would not have been let in by our police without a letter of this nature. At the time it wasn't the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that was in charge of refugee issues, but rather our office. That is why the UNHCR turned to us and they received permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at another document, 1D 01 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, we've just seen a document that confirms the explanations you gave us earlier on and we are not talking here about assumptions. We have evidence that the UNHCR was requesting transit visas from the office -- yes, yes, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, had I been given this document earlier, it would have been clearer sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but with regard to the 500 people from Mostar, did you have a document from the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't know that since I did not sign that document. I probably wasn't even in Zagreb even. I was either abroad attending a meeting in Geneva or in Strasbourg or I wasn't in the office in that period for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The witness has clarified it, Your Honour. There's no connection between this transaction and the 500 people from Mostar, so it's a complete -- still an assumption. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to skip one document and just to pick up where you left off, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the next series of documents 1D 02601, we see at the very top, and this is dated 26th September 1994 at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner. The next document, 1D 02600, 29 September 1994 at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner, again we see your name at the bottom. 1D 02599, at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner, again we see your name, this is dated 5 October 1994. 1D 02598, 17 October 1994, at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner, we see your name again there and we see that this is I think 56 people. 1D 02597, this is 18 October 1994, at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner, again we see your name there. 1D 02596, at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner, this is dated 20 October 1994, we see your name. 1D 02594, 31 October 1994, at the request of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. Then we go to again 31 October 1994, this is document 1D 02595. And lastly we see 2 November 1994 in document 1D 02593, we see your name again. Dr. Rebic, having looked at all of these documents where your name is mentioned, are you familiar with these documents and --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with these documents, although some were signed for me. All those documents were sent to important figures, such as the vice prime minister of Croatia, as well as Mr. Hajker Hajnan [phoen], who was deputy head for the UNHCR; it was sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; the Ministry of the Interior in the border area; and to the archives. These documents prove as to the lawful conduct of the office which acted within the international and domestic legislation. We were allowed to give permission for transit of those people before their removal to third countries and to accommodate them in the interim. Before going there, they had to transit via Croatia, and in that case the UNHCR sought permission from our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to turn your attention to one document that we did skip, purposely, that is, 1D 01582, so you have to go back a little bit, sir, 1582. This is dated 26 -- April 26, 1994. We see your name at the bottom. This is a letter from the Government of Republic of Croatia to a Mr. Fischer, and it says: "Surviving winter office Fischer."

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Mr. Karnavas, I see the document. Mr. Fischer dealt with relocation of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to third countries. They always transited through Croatia, since there was no other possibility. Since the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in our conversations mentioned it to me, and they told me that this gentleman should be warned, I told Mr. Fischer that in the future when removing citizens of the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- through our territory they need to ask permission through the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereupon I would issue permission for transit. This document proves --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here because I want to go slowly step by step. Paragraph number 2, let's focus here for a second. It says: "Namely, due to the frequent complaints from the Bosnian and Herzegovinian authorities, claiming that this office together with international humanitarian organizations is helping the Serbians in the 'ethnic cleansing' of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in accordance with the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, international humanitarian organizations must submit with the request for acquiring permits for transit through the Republic of Croatia a written consent from the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb." Why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary in order to avoid such misunderstandings as the ones we could just see concerning the ODPR. Thanks to the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their complaints and in cooperation with them, we acted upon it. As much as we could, we tried to control the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina transiting through Croatia on to third countries. I can say that there were many people who were doing it without our knowledge, and at the border our police would stop such people whereupon I had to intervene in order to either allow them transit or to keep them in the Republic of Croatia and to give them refugee status since third countries would not receive them. Slovenia, for instance, there were cases in which the Slovenian police would not receive them but return them to Croatia, and as of that moment they were in our charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at -- if we skip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we'll have to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just need one question and then the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we skip one paragraph: "We would like to point out that it would also be necessary as it has been up to now that you submit a valid letter of guarantee for each person individually as well as pay the administrative tax." Why was that necessary, for him to submit a valid letter of guarantee?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary so that the office would know who should be paid expenses since there were many people appearing who asked the office to pay for certain expenses without the office knowing who they were. That is why this was asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had there been abuses as far as letters of guarantees, in other words, phoney ones? Had there been that had come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there had been abuses. There were forgeries. There was one person from the ODPR whom I fired because that person worked with an institution in Banja Luka. He or she forged my signature and illegally used the stamp; therefore, I had to fire that person. I was sorry to do that, but that person acted illegally. Unfortunately, there were abuses which were difficult to deal with. On occasion, however, we sometimes succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so just one final point. If the letter of guarantee was forged, then it would mean that once they came into Croatia, Croatia was stuck with them? Is that what you've been telling us?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Croatia had to take them in and take care of them; there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we shall check the time you have left. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. The registrar is telling me that you have 27 minutes left. So failing any procedural matters or over-lengthy questions by the Judges, you may be able to complete your direct today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go to binder number 3 for you, sir, and I'm looking at P 03765, P 03765. And in order to fully appreciate this, everyone should be looking also -- should look at or glance at P 03708, which is what is being referred to in the letter by Ms. Turkovic. Focusing on P 03765, she indicated to you, she says in the third paragraph: "Mr. Rebic, you are reproaching me that, I as Ambassador Of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did not show any interest in Croat people expelled from the Lasva valley, whereby you again used wrong information. "With regard to that, I would like to stress that immediately after the arrival of refugees from the Central Bosnia, I went to Poljud to visit them, I issued order to secure supplies for those people from the Logistic Centre in Split, I organized provision of bread and worked hard to enable their transfer to a better accommodation facility." Now, with respect to the expelled people, the Croats that were expelled from the Lasva valley, to your knowledge and understanding, is Ms. Turkovic correct when she said she had visited them?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I don't remember that Ms. Bisera Turkovic, with whom I had a very good relationship, was ever in Split to receive these refugees from Lasva valley, but I know well that I had to urgently take a flight -- a private flight on a Croatian army aircraft to Split in order to deal with the issue of these refugees. To cut a long story short, they had been expelled from Lasva valley in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and arrived in Split. And in Split they did not want to take accommodation that was offered to them on the island -- on the peninsula of Peljesac. I asked the ministry of defence to provide us with a military accommodation there, and they gave us a military holiday resort called Perma [phoen] on the peninsula of Peljesac. They didn't want to go there, they wanted to remain in Split, but there was no room in Split, and they insisted on being accommodated in a hotel but the hotels, they were all full. There was a tug of war. I spent some very difficult hours with them. There was a Franciscan monk with them who kept on insisting that the people remain in Split instead of going to Perma. I appealed to his conscience. I appealed to his sense and sensibility. He finally caved in, and all these refugees were sent to Perma. At that moment, nobody in Split, none of the refugees or the Franciscan monk, ever mentioned Ms. Bisera Turkovic, so there was no way for me to know that she had been down there. And I have serious doubts about the fact that she may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how far is the place where they went from Split?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By ferry it takes approximately three-quarters of an hour, 45 minutes approximately, depending on weather conditions. By road it takes a bit longer because you have to go from Split towards Dubrovnik, and then cross to the peninsula of Peljesac and the journey lasts about an hour and a half. The accommodation there was okay, but it's a good illustration to show that sometimes people were dissatisfied with accommodation irrespective of their origin. I had occasional problems with both Muslims and Croats, refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In this instance it appears, at least from you are telling us, the Franciscan was the one that was -- that you were negotiating with?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I implored with him to understand the situation, to understand the seriousness of the situation, and to try and talk to people and lead them to Perma to the military holiday resort and finally they accepted that, and they all headed for Perma in quite a good mood and peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 01432. You have to skip a few documents because due to time we're going to skip through some of these documents. It's 1D 01432.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 932?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1432. It looks -- it may look like a 9 but it should be a 4.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay, okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we see that -- are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with this document, indeed. It was sent by Bosnia and Herzegovina -- actually, by the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna to the Government of the Republic of Croatia to Deputy Prime Minister Mr. Kostovic and other responsible persons, including myself. And this document is actually a request to register a representative office of the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Darinko Tadic requested that in order to register a representative office of the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees of the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let me stop you here. At a time there was an embassy for Bosnia-Herzegovina, presumably for all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Zagreb. We see correspondence from Turkovic and her associate Krajsek complaining about one ethnicity primarily in respect to two particular sites. Why would it be necessary to open up such a representative office for the Croats if you had an embassy in Zagreb for Bosnia-Herzegovina, presumably for everybody?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know why such a representative office should be registered. The Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees with the Government of the Republic of Croatia should have sufficed. As for dealing with refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina of Croatian ethnic origin, it was the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was competent. When it came to the refugee issues of refugees of Croatian ethnicity, we dealt with them in the same way as we did in the case of Bosniak Muslims. This was all done in our office, so I'm really not sure what the purpose would have been of registering an office of that kind. And on top of that, in Herceg-Bosna there was an Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees that was already mentioned earlier today. We tried to support that office logistically to get the people there started in their new job. In the same way I helped citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina of Muslim origin. Mrs. Omerbasic spent several days in my office and she was introduced to the job. She was told how to establish such an office in Sarajevo. In other words, I helped both sides, I helped the ones as I did the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to the next document, as 1D 02277. And at the very top we see: "Refugee settlement Pineta," and look at the third paragraph -- or fourth, it says: "12.000 Croats were forced to leave Kakanj municipality and they are now in Capljina, Stolac, Pocitelj, Ljubusko, Lipovljani, Bjelolasica, Klana," and so on and then we see Pineta. And it says: "There are 1300 of us in Pineta where we have organized our lives ..." Could you please tell us what Pineta was?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pineta is or was a holiday complex with bungalows near Novi Grad in the vicinity of Slovenian border, and it was owned by a Slovenian company. This is where refugees of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mostly from Vares and Kakanj, were accommodated in the bungalows there. They were also accommodated in other places because there was a huge number of them, maybe 12.000 of them, who were Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina and who had been forced to come to Croatia and seek the refugee status there. Therefore, they were accommodated in other refugee centres, in Bjelolasica, Lipovljani, and Klana near Rijeka, and Selce, and in Pineta, as you said it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there ever a problem with the refugees that were staying in Pineta?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, there was a problem, a rather big one for the refugees themselves, the problem that made the refugees very nervous and was a constant source of stress. The Slovenian company asked us to move the refugees out from that holiday complex so that their guests could be accommodated there as tourists. I would reply to the Slovenians, telling them that I wasn't able to do that because there was no other way for me to accommodate these people. Pineta was my only solution. I proposed that they should take the refugees over and accommodate them in Slovenia and look after them there, but they were adamant in saying, No, no way. Then I asked them to help us build something as a temporary solution and then they refused that as well. I asked what then? They said, Move them out. I said, How can I move them out? I can't just have them end up in the street. That was the problem in Pineta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me stop you here. If I understand it correctly, this is a private enterprise owned by private individuals, not the Government of Slovenia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a company, yes, but it was not a corporation but it was a legal subject with a lot of employees and workers who had been used to spending their summer holidays there. As I sit here today I really can't remember what the name of that enterprise was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's set aside the entrepreneurs who have to make a profit through the use of these enterprises. Did the Government of Slovenia ever intervene on behalf of the enterprise to get the Croatian government to evict the refugees that were located in Pineta?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember today, 12 or 13 years after the event, the company appealed to the Government of the Republic of Slovenia, asking them to take steps. I received a proposal by the Government of the Republic of Slovenia, asking me to deal with the issue in favour of the company. If there was no other way to deal with it, that I should reach an agreement with the company and put a time bar on the use of Pineta by refugees. It all ended by us signing an agreement with the company, but we were not able to meet any dead-lines because at the time all of our possibilities had been exhausted and we could not accommodate the refugees anywhere else. There were just no other possibilities. That's why we kept them there for a little while longer, and I believe that this issue dragged on even after I left the office and it was finally solved only five or six years ago. People simply could not return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their houses in Kakanj and Vares had been destroyed. I visited them. They all pleaded stress, terrible events, and they had seen the Mujahedin there, that they had been slaughtered by the soldiers of the Bosnian army. In other words, all these people were stressed out and their stories were not the easiest and the nicest stories to listen to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to 1D 00927, 927, and it would appear that this -- if we look at page 2 that this -- this letter was delivered to the Office of Refugees and Displaced Persons of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, that's what it says. Do you recall receiving this letter from Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I received the letter at the time. It was copied to me, and I was prepared to receive him just like I did everybody else from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, should that be necessary. In the letter Dr. Prlic states that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna could not provide for such a large number of people, and in that case if they could not care for the people they would send them to us and we were supposed to look for them because we were the first country point where they sought protection and we were obliged to provide it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Now, do you recall whether they -- these folks came to the Republic of Croatia; and if so, where did they end up?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are precisely those people that we have just discussed. Those people came from Kakanj and Vares and were accommodated in the Republic of Croatia in Pineta, on Mount Bjelolasica, in Lipovljani and in other refugee centres depending on the available accommodation. We had one in Pula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to need on to the next topic, and I would direct your attention to 1D 01320, 1D 01320. And if you find it, I'm interested in the second page, of course. We see from the cover page it's from the Ivo Komsic's book: "Who, when, and where divided BiH." And we see if we turn to the first page September 14, 1993, a joint declaration. And if we look at under I, paragraph number 2, it says: "Ensure mutual and unconditional disbandment of all prisoner camps and the release of all prisoners on the territories under the control of the armies of BiH and HVO, immediately and not later than September 21, 1993, at 12.00 noon, with the mutual acceptance of responsibility for their protection and care." And if we could go to the last page for everyone's attention because the issue has been raised as to why certain individuals were involved, we see here the President, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, had appointed for his commissioner, Dr. Mate Granic, Vice-President of the government and minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of Croatia, and then we see that Haris Silajdzic is appointed by Izetbegovic for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you aware of this joint declaration signed September 14, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of this declaration. This declaration made it easier upon ourselves because we heard that in keeping with that joint declaration the unwanted conflicts would finally stop between the two victims of the war, between Bosniak Muslims and Bosniak Croats, Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01936, and we see at the very end on page 3 we see that this is from Dr. Haris Silajdzic, but on the first page we see your name, the visit to Klaka and Varazdin. Do you recall that visit?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do indeed, Mr. Karnavas. I remember the visit. I was there on several occasions with Mr. Sevko Omerbasic, the religious leader of Muslims in Croatia. I visited refugee centres, Klaka and Varazdin are mentioned here. Varazdin had two large refugee centres that accommodated Muslims [as interpreted]. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at the very first paragraph we see that this is: "In connection with application of the joint declaration by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the president of the Republic of Croatia." Now --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm being told that it should say Muslim refugees on page 84, line 1 and 2. Did you ever visit Dretelj? Did you visit Dretelj yourself?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been -- I should actually consult my agenda, but this must have been in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was this in connection with the joint declaration?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a serious attempt on the part of the Republic of Croatia to help Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, more completely, those in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and deal once and for all with the consequences of that conflict. When we learned in Zagreb that there was some detainees, military prisoners in Dretelj, former members of the either the HVO or the Bosnian army, I can't remember at this point which, then President Tudjman ordered Granic to immediately go there in keeping with the joint declaration and see what was going on down there. A year -- a day or two before Granic had sent some people there to be his scouts, and when they returned they informed him that the situation was, indeed, very serious. Then Stante Pede [phoen], Granic, and I went down there to resolve the problem of Dretelj by a way of ordering Dretelj to be closed down with immediate effect and Granic told people there then that Dretelj should be closed down immediately and that all those who were there would be accepted by the Republic of Croatia and would be given refugee status there. We asked for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I requested an additional hour. I had indicated that I needed five hours with this witness, and also there were two other witnesses to follow where we originally had scheduled for eight hours and I reduced them to six hours. So I would need for the rest of the day to finish up. I have one more topic and it deals with returns because there's been some -- the gentleman was involved with the return situation and there's been an allegation that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you are aware that the other Defence teams will have two hours and that the Prosecution will have four hours. Considering procedural incidents that are very numerous and considering Judges' questions, the witness is likely to have to come back next week. That's the problem here. That's the risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's any assistance, I can say that there would be no cross-examination on behalf of Bruno Stojic. I don't know if that helps the Court in its scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can tell you that General Petkovic's Defence will have a few questions for this witness, but very few, so we will not use all of our time. So if it's of any assistance to the Defence of Mr. Prlic, we will only be glad to give him our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid any dilemmas, General Praljak's defence will need 15 minute, not more, unless something else crops up and this will be our cross-examination. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric's Defence will not have any questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Pusic's Defence does not intend to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I see that the other Defence teams will need 20 to 25 minutes. If you are granted 20 additional minutes, the Prosecution will have four hours and 20 minutes to cross-examine the witness, but I'll ask my fellow Judges if they agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time you're going to use now will also be granted to the Prosecution in addition to the four hours they had in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine, Mr. President. We never objected to the Prosecution having all the time they need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to 1D 02735 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I know that we are pressed by time, but the -- since I do not want to ask a question about a document which was just penultimate question asked by you, therefore I would like to ask Dr. Rebic about the following. You presented him with document 1D 01320 which was written, I believe, by Ivo Komsic, I mean the whole book, but you referred to a joint declaration in that document, a joint declaration by Izetbegovic and Tudjman, that is between President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman, on September 14, 1993. Now, my question is that when you presented this one to Dr. Rebic, you asked really about the issue of the refugees and displaced persons from BiH and et cetera, and I of course also know and Dr. Rebic has mentioned that he himself was not there and he doesn't seem to be added to the signatories to that declaration, that is from the Croatian side, Hrvoje Sarinic, Zeljko Matic, Miomir Zuzul, and Hidajet Biscevic. My question is frankly the following, I am a bit surprised that in this joint declaration there is not -- there is no reference made to the government or HVO or the government of the -- of that time in Herzegovina and there was no mentioning -- there is no mentioning of anything as far as their cooperation or their role in the presentation of this declaration. So my question is to Dr. Rebic is if he has any knowledge about the implementation of the declaration and about the role which might have been played by the Government of Herceg-Bosna. Officially probably it was not the name at the time in 1993, but anyway they had to play a role in the implementation of the declaration, which is my question, Dr. Rebic. What kind of role should have been played by the HVO and by the Government of Herceg-Bosna, and do you know if there was any involvement by them in the implementation of the declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by virtue of my office I was not part of that; therefore, I cannot provide any details in terms of an answer to your question. My field was a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record we see that this is in keeping with the principles of the London Conference, Your Honour, and the purpose, for the record and for your purposes, given that the Prosecution alleges that Croatia was involved in the joint criminal enterprise and questions why they are involved, we see a joint declaration and that's the purpose of this. And of course we're connecting it with 1D 01936 because it does say that Mr. Rebic's -- Dr. Rebic's involvement in Dretelj was in connection with the application of the joint declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I can just now turn to the next document, 1D 02735, we see this is a copy of a newspaper article dated 26th September 1993, it says: "Prisoners become refugees." Are you familiar with -- we see that you're mentioned. Are you familiar with this article and does this article more or less comport with the facts?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with it. This article reflects the facts. This has to do with the people who were in Dretelj through UNHCR mediation and with the assistance of the ICRC they were transferred to Croatia. We received them and accommodate them in Korcula and on the island of Badija. We granted them refugee status immediately and we treated them as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we go to the final chapter is -- deals with returns. And if you could tell us again what the policy was as far as returning refugees back from the Republic of Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, what was the process? And if you could be ever so brief.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process was in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and in agreement with the UNHCR when individual areas, be it in the Republic of Croatia when talking about displaced persons, be it in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina when we're talking about refugees, were liberated, when they were free of any threat of war, then we gradually returned DPs and refugees to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The instruction in place by our office was distributed to our regional offices to return only those people who are going back to a safe area in which houses were habitable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The refugee status is being extended to those who were unable to return to those who were sick, to the parents whose children were attending schools, and that instruction was familiar to my regional office; however, the -- they did not act as strictly uniformly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But there was no policy to just simply return people if the conditions were not appropriate?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. If there were no adequate conditions, we were not allowed to return those people. However, it frequently had to do with people who enjoyed refugee status in Croatia and had their homes in Bosnia-Herzegovina in completely safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Before I go to the next document, in your report: "My work at the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees," and we don't need to get it but this is 1D 02921, you indicate at one point on page 33 - and I'll just read it - that on -- let's say: "On 22nd August I met Urs Betschart Swiss, deputy minister for refugees, and Peter Haeller, his associate. They requested that Croatia urgently take back 300 refugees from Croatia and 10.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina because they had Croatian passports." Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Switzerland did have a certain number of refugees from Croatia and from Bosnia and Herzegovina and at any cost they wanted to see them returned to the Republic of Croatia. In that particular case it was a large number of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, out of which a large portion had Croatian passports. They were aware that they had the right to return such refugees to the Republic of Croatia since Croatia had to take care of its citizens, i.e., of those to whom it had issued passports, irrespective of whether they were Christians or Muslims, or that is to say whether they were Bosniak Muslims or Croatians from Bosnia. The fact that they had Croatian passports made it our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you this though, on this occasion, and I know that you've indicated that Germany was the same, you said that yesterday, but I just want to ask you.
