Did the representatives from Switzerland ever inquire as to how possible was it for those individuals to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina or was it -- were they leaving it up to Croatia to determine how and when and under what conditions the 10.000 Bosnian refugees with Croatian passports would get back to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left it to the Republic of Croatia to take care of those people and to either return them to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or if that proved impossible to keep them in Croatia and take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 01798, we're going to go through several documents rather quickly. This is a letter to the Bosnian and Herzegovinian embassy in Zagreb and it's a report on the implementation of the programme for the return of refugees and expelled persons from the Kingdom of Denmark to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did your office by any chance have to get involved with the return of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina that had gone to Denmark?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly before that the Republic of Croatia was visited by Minister Birte Weiss who was a minister in the Danish government. She let us know that the Danish government had decided that it had been taking care of refugees for a sufficient amount of time and that they needed to be returned. She also said that among them there were those who wanted to go back and they were looking for a possibility of doing so. I agreed with Minister Birte Weiss on that because there was no other way for me. If the Danish government was sending their refugees back, we had to take them in following the same procedure. If they were Croatian citizens, they were to remain in the Republic of Croatia; if they were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were to continue their travel onwards to that country. If unable to return there, they were to stop in Croatia where they were supposed to receive refugee status for as long as their return to Bosnia-Herzegovina is arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 02591 and if we can recall yesterday you indicated that at some point, I believe it was yesterday that you said, that there was some sort of an agreement that you signed on behalf of the Government of the Republic of Croatia with the -- with Germany.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It had to do with a gradual and organized return of 35 [as interpreted] refugees who were from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and were in Germany at the time. Mr. Manfred Kanther, who was the minister of the interior, signed a protocol with me under which the return was to take place. We attached to it a list of all available places to which the citizens could return, but we asked them to keep for a while those refugees who were unable to go back to the locations which we attached as well and which were still under occupation either in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina, making their return impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could look at the next three documents very quickly, I just want you to look at them and then I'll have one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a little precision again. The witness spoke of 35 refugees and that's what's in the record. If one looks at the document one finds the figure six -- five pages from the bottom of 35.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I thought I heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, I said 35.000, 35.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The transcript will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's page 92, line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You find 35 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've heard 35.000 and sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I heard 35 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at -- and I appreciate that, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02620, and then with that if you look at 1D 02621 and 1D 02619, if you just look at them very quickly, in relation to your previous answer you had indicated, as I understand, that the agreement was that locations that had been designated as safe areas from those -- refugees from those areas could be returned on a gradual basis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you tell us for the record what these documents reflect, that is, 1D 02620, 2621, and 2619?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list of all places and settlements that was sent to all regional offices, all 21 of them, and to all centres for social welfare of which there were over 200. The list contains the names of all places to which return was possible. That is why the regional offices and centres for social welfare had to abide by it. They were supposed to send only those DPs and refugees who hailed from these locations which were free at the time. It was in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, I want to thank you very, very much for your testimony and for coming here and thank you for being honest and forthright. We would ask that you would do so with the Prosecution and with anyone else asking you any questions while you're here in The Hague. Thank you very, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well. Thank you as well, Professor Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, you will return in this courtroom tomorrow afternoon for the rest of your testimony. Questions will be put to you by the Defences of General Praljak and of Mr. Petkovic. The Praljak Defence told us that they would need 15 minutes and the Petkovic Defence will have just a few questions to put to you. After that, the Prosecution will cross-examine you for about four hours and 20 minutes. The registrar will give me the exact time later on. We'll see each other again tomorrow. No need for me to tell you that you're not to have any contact with anyone because you are a witness of the Tribunal. That's something I've already mentioned, I believe. I wish you a very pleasant evening. It's almost 7.00 p.m., and we'll resume the proceedings tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
